content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
Main comments:
This paper proposes a unified embedding for image classification and instance retrieval. The objectives for both classification and retrieval are jointly optimized. To bridge the gap between image classification and instance retrieval, the generalized mean pooling layer with exponent p is proposed. A repeated batch sampling augmentation is introduced to enhance the performance for both tasks.

Those schemes proposed in this paper are shown to be effective through extensive experiments. However, those schemes are more like good techniques to improve the performance instead of bridging the gap between two tasks, rather than principled algorithm designs.

Overall, this paper proposes several schemes including self-supervision, generalized mean pooling, and repeated augmentation to improve the performance of two tasks. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of those schemes. However, those schemes are more like techniques to improve the performance instead of bridging the gap between two tasks. Another possible explanation is the gap between image classification and instance retrieval is not as large as stated. It is important to justify the claims how those schemes bridge the gap between image classification and instance retrieval in a principle manner (rather than good techniques or tricks).

The p in the proposed GeM seems has limited influence on both classification and retrieval. AAs shown in Fig.2, except for p=1, the performance of p with other values are similar. The authors mentioned that the GeM is a trade-off for between average pooling and max pooling, why not just use two different pooling ops for two tasks. Maybe GeM is a trick for preserving more local information, but I cannot tell its advantage for balancing two tasks. And the optimal p in GeM is obtained by grid search, which makes me double the real value of GeM.

The authors mentioned that image resolution used for classification and retrieval is quite different. It is not clear whether the gap between those two tasks is mainly because that the backbone network is not capable of capturing details. This needs to be addressed. In addition, there have been several methods that aim to capture both details and global features [1-3] by designing backbone networks with multi-scale ability

[1] Big-little net: An efficient multi-scale feature representation for visual and speech recognition
[2] Res2Net: A New Multi-scale Backbone Architecture
[3] Deep High-Resolution Representation Learning for Visual Recognition

The authors need to put this work in proper context and discuss the differences. It is also better to add more experimental evaluations against these methods to clearly demonstrate the merits of this work.

content.title: Response to reviewer #2
content.comment:
We thank reviewer #2 for his comments and suggestions. We agree with the reviewer that the gap between image classification and retrieval is probably not as big as one might expect. However, we think this is a direct conclusion of our work, rather than what can be inferred from the existing literature. Indeed, we think there is merit in showing both that using a self-supervised retrieval loss boosts classification accuracies at no extra data-labeling cost; and that doing so yields a joint embedding that is competitive with the state-of-the art in classification and image retrieval.
	In our experiments, we show that the p-exponent adaptation scheme does have significant impact. As mentioned in the text, and as an example, adapting the p-exponent at resolution 500 yields to a classification accuracy gain of +0.6%, which is significant in regard of existing literature experimenting on ImageNet.
We have presented our results at different image resolutions in order to offer direct comparisons both with the classification literature, as well as with the retrieval literature. As shown in our experiments, intermediate scales (s*=500) offer good performance both in classification and retrieval and align with our goal of using a single embedding for the two tasks. We believe considering multi-scale backbones are interesting extensions but is beyond the scope of our work, which addresses preexisting questions with respect to bridging classification and image retrieval tasks.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The paper proposes to jointy train a deep neural net for image classification, instance and copy recognition. This is achieved by i) combining a classification (cross-entropy) loss with a retrieval loss based on multiple copies/augmentations of the training image, and ii) a generalized mean pooling (GeM) layer allowing to interpolate between average and max pooling. The network obtains improved image classification accuracy on ImageNet over the same model trained without additional losses, and retrieval results competitive with the state of the art.

The paper is well-written and the different components are well explained. The improvements obtained on ImageNet are considerable, and I like the idea of using the GeM layer pooling exponent to adapt the network to higher resolutions. Also, it is desirable to have models that work well on multiple tasks e.g. for deployment on mobile devices.

I have several questions and concerns:

- Repeated augmentation together with a retrieval loss as the one presented in (2) is a known supervised learning technique called exemplar [1], which was originally proposed with a classification loss but recently extended to a to a triplet loss as the one in (2) in [2]. The same loss was also used together with labels for semi-supervised learning in [3], and similar improvements in image classification accuracy as in the proposed paper were observed for training a rotation-based self-supervised loss with all labels (the MOAM model in [3]). I think the paper would benefit from a review of recent work on self-supervised learning.

- It was previously observed that increasing the resolution can improve image classification accuracy, see, e.g. in [5, 4]. It is also to be expected that adding AutoAugment to the mix will help.

- It would be interesting to see a simple ImageNet pretrained retrieval baseline without bells and whistles in the retrieval experiments. I’m not a retrieval expert, but it seems that retrieval networks are typically trained on other data sets and do additional tricks than just using a pretrained ImageNet embedding.

All in all I think the paper is solid and presents good results, but a very similar method was previously proposed by [3]. I’m therefore not convinced that the paper presents enough novelty.

Minor comment:
-Using a different letter for the supervised labels y_j and the pairwise labels y_ij might improve readability.


[1] Dosovitskiy A, Springenberg JT, Riedmiller M, Brox T. Discriminative unsupervised feature learning with convolutional neural networks. In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 2014 (pp. 766-774).
[2] Kolesnikov A, Zhai X, Beyer L. Revisiting Self-Supervised Visual Representation Learning. InProceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition 2019 (pp. 1920-1929).
[3] Zhai X, Oliver A, Kolesnikov A, Beyer L. S4L: Self-Supervised Semi-Supervised Learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:1905.03670. 2019 May 9.
[4] Tan M, Le QV. EfficientNet: Rethinking Model Scaling for Convolutional Neural Networks. arXiv preprint arXiv:1905.11946. 2019 May 28.
[5] Touvron H, Vedaldi A, Douze M, Jégou H. Fixing the train-test resolution discrepancy. arXiv preprint arXiv:1906.06423. 2019 Jun 14.

content.title: Response to reviewer #3
content.comment:
We thank reviewer #3 for his comments and suggestions. We address his comments as follows:

- We thank the reviewer for the literature on self-supervised methods. We agree that the reference [3] is closest to our method, in that it combines a self-supervised signal with a classification task. We note however that their 80.17% MOAM accuracy when training with all labels is obtained on a ResNet-v2 4x wider, which makes direct comparison difficult. Moreover, we bring further additional contributions in our work: first, showing that the RA scheme is beneficial in itself, regardless of the retrieval loss; second, and more importantly, evaluating our approach specifically in a retrieval setting and reaching new state-of-the art on unsupervised retrieval baselines.

- It is to be expected that deeper networks trained on images with higher input resolution yields better results. But we show that by adjusting the p exponent at test-time, we can evaluate on larger scale images *without retraining the weights*. This has practical applications, as inference is typically less resource-intensive than training.

- Retrieval experiments on pretrained networks are present in Annex E, following the exact same evaluation procedure as our MultiGrain networks (in particulat with respect to whitening). Overall, we show retrieval improvements both over these baselines and over other unsupervised methods. As suggested by the reviewer, supervised retrieval exists, but is a different task: in our case, we aim to reach a good retrieval performance accross datasets, ensuring out-of-domain generalization.

In conclusion, we respectfully disagree regarding the lack of novelty compared to [3], and stress that retrieval is a different problem than semi-supervised learning and presents real challenges, which makes the competitivity of our single-embedding approach with previous unsupervised retrieval methods particularly attractive.

content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I did not assess the derivations or theory.
content.review:
The authors present a new neural network method for generating image embeddings which can be used for image classification and instance retrieval. It seems to be implemented using a combination of existing techniques such as CNNs and generalized mean pooling. The model has to linear heads to do classification and image retrieval. The authors obtain new state of the art results on classification when compared to previous results obtained with similar architectures.

Novelty:

I believe this is the main limitation of this work. It seems the proposed method does not have significant innovations and it is obtained from combining previous methodologies.

Quality and significance:

The experiments seem to indicate that the proposed method could be useful in practice. However, the lack of new methodological contributions reduces the quality and significance of this work.

Clarity:

The paper seems to be clearly written and is easy to read.

content.title: Response to reviewer #1
content.comment: We thank reviewer #1 for his comments; we respectfully ask him to reconsider the novelty aspect given the argumentation of our general remark above. We believe we do have several methodological contributions, including: GeM for classification, joint training, repeated augmentations, p-exponent adjustment; as well as an answer to an important computer vision question: showing that classification and retrieval are compatible tasks, and that a joint training can improve on both tasks.

replying_to: Replying to MultiGrain: a unified image embedding for classes and instances

content.title: General comment
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their comments.
Several reviewers have assessed that our work presents little novelty, which we disagree with. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to address the jointly training a network for image classification and retrieval. These tasks have been disjoint fields for a decade. We hope that the readers appreciate the practical importance of having a unique backbone for both tasks.
Jointly tackling the two tasks while achieving state-of-the-art results on both is far from trivial, as indicated by the architectural difference in their respective “best practice” in Table 1.

To achieve that, we introduce several new practices: to our knowledge GeM has not been used successfully for classification in the deep-learning era; incorporating data augmentation in the contrastive loss as a supervision signal to do jointly instance search and classification is also new.

Our work also uncovered more broadly useful and unknown techniques: we show that the repeated augmentation batching strategy improves image classification with a cross-entropy loss, and we propose a scale-adaptive test-time adjustment of pooling exponents that is extremely effective and, we believe, of broad interest.

We stress that the overall +0.6 to +1.8% absolute ImageNet improvements we obtain using networks trained with same amount of supervision, same backbone and same training resolution are very significant with regard to improvements commonly reported in image classification.
